item.title: Portable 'Wi-Fi' terminals help China's military units maintain battlefield connectivity on the move
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-22 21:11:00
Photo: PLA Daily A lightweight communication terminal, weighing less than 3 kilograms, is helping Chinese military units maintain communication links - like a portable Wi-Fi - as they maneuver between battlefield positions, offering a more flexible alternative to the time-consuming deployment of traditional communication cables, read a PLA Daily report on Sunday. The portable network and communications terminal, developed by a unit of the People's Liberation Army (PLA) Information Support Force, can be rapidly deployed to establish wireless connections between command terminals and frontline units, allowing information to be transmitted without waiting for communication cables to be laid again after a position change. In a recent joint training exercise, a PLA Air Force firepower unit received an order to relocate shortly after having completed a round of live-fire exercises. While a communications support team was preparing to carry conventional fiber-optic cables to the new position, an advance team reported that the portable terminal had already been set up, with the command communications link established. By the time the cable-laying team arrived, the firepower unit had completed a simulated strike and was preparing to move again, the PLA Daily reported. The development addresses a long-standing challenge in battlefield communications support. Under traditional arrangements, communications personnel had to retrieve and re-deploy cables whenever combat units changed positions, a process that required considerable manpower and time and could leave units temporarily without communications. Military commentator Song Zhongping told the Global Times on Sunday that mobile networking can significantly improve the speed and flexibility of communications support compared with conventional cable-based deployment. "Mobile networking, as the name suggests, means no longer having to lay extensive networks of cables as was traditionally done. The traditional approach consumes considerable manpower, material resources and financial resources, while its efficiency and ability to respond rapidly are limited," Song told the Global Times. By deploying mobile communications equipment, including base stations, military units can establish communications and command networks more quickly and move these capabilities to areas where they are needed, Song noted. "For a military force to respond rapidly, what needs to come first is not just logistics, but also command and communications," Song said. "Without that, it is impossible to achieve connectivity and interoperability across the entire force." According to the PLA Daily report, the portable terminals can be deployed at multiple locations to form a mobile networking cluster, rather than relying on a single communications node or fixed position. During another training exercise involving the seizure of key positions, an advance unit maneuvered through difficult terrain and areas with dense electromagnetic interference. Using multiple portable terminals, the unit established a mobile network while moving and filled gaps in communications coverage. When a reconnaissance team identified a simulated enemy firepower position, target information was transmitted through the mobile network to several dispersed firepower units. The units then coordinated their simulated strikes based on a shared, real-time operational picture. The communications links remained operational throughout the exercise, the PLA Daily report said. Song said the use of multiple interconnected nodes can improve the resilience of battlefield communications by providing redundancy. "Communications on the battlefield cannot rely entirely on a single node. Multiple nodes are needed, with several portable mobile communications terminals deployed redundantly to ensure that the entire communications network remains secure and reliable," Song told the Global Times. However, the shift toward wireless networking also brings security challenges that cannot be overlooked. Song noted that wireless communications inevitably involve the transmission of radio signals, creating the possibility that communications could be intercepted or information disclosed. Encryption and other security safeguards are therefore essential to mobile military communications systems. "How to prevent information from being leaked is the core challenge facing mobile and network-based communications," he said. The PLA Daily report also stressed that the portable terminals are not intended to replace wired communications. Instead, the unit is exploring a complementary model combining fixed and mobile systems: Wired networks are used at established positions, where reliability and resistance to interference are priorities, while portable equipment is deployed for temporary maneuvers and field operations, where rapid setup and filling coverage gaps are more important. The unit has also incorporated challenging conditions, including strong electromagnetic interference and difficult terrain, into routine training to test equipment performance and refine its networking methods. Looking ahead, Song said military communications systems would continue to evolve alongside advances in technology, with more sophisticated encryption methods and new forms of portable, distributed communications equipment potentially improving their security and reliability. "New technologies will continue to replace older ones, but the ultimate goal remains ensuring that communications are reliable and secure, with security always coming first," he said.

item.title: PLA Army steps up training with new-generation 8x8 armored vehicles featuring enhanced firepower, protection
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-22 21:02:00
Several new-generation 8x8 armored vehicles move across the ground. Photo: Screenshot from CCTV News' military channel China's new-generation 8x8 wheeled infantry fighting vehicle has drawn attention after footage of the new armored vehicle in use during the People's Liberation Army (PLA) 83rd Group Army training was released by official media on Friday. Experts noted that it has improved upon its predecessor, the Type 08 family, particularly in defensive and information systems. Its upgrades are expected to improve the sustained combat capabilities and survivability of the PLA's medium combined-arms brigades. The footage comes as the PLA Army has stepped up its training with the newly introduced equipment. A brigade of the PLA Army's 83rd Group Army recently organized intensive training for more than 100 personnel, focusing on combat driving of the new armored vehicles and small-unit tactics, according to a report by state broadcaster CCTV News on Friday. "The new equipment has a higher level of informatization and greater speed. Everyone in the unit is determined to master it," Zheng Tao, a member of the brigade, was quoted as saying in the CCTV report. With no established training materials available for the new equipment, the brigade set up specialized research teams to tackle technical challenges, Zheng said. Personnel have been learning through training, summarizing their experiences and working collectively to resolve problems, he said. The new 8x8 infantry fighting vehicle has appeared in several official media reports throughout 2026. In January, CCTV reported on a coordinated tactical exercise involving an armored infantry squad from a PLA Army's 76th Group Army brigade, marking the vehicle's first public appearance. A CCTV report in June outlined several features of the new vehicle, including high mobility and speed, an unmanned turret, improved crew protection, amphibious capabilities and vehicle-mounted anti-tank missiles. It also highlighted a flexible rear door that can open either sideways or downward. In August, CCTV News released footage showing a PLA Army's 76th Group Army brigade conducting coordinated training with the new 8x8 wheeled infantry fighting vehicles in Northwest China's Gobi Desert. Multiple vehicles were seen moving across rough terrain and coordinating with ground troops during tactical exercises. A key upgrade of the new infantry fighting vehicle is its unmanned turret, which allows all crew members to remain inside the vehicle's hull while operating its weapons, significantly improving crew protection. The vehicle seems to be equipped with a longer-barreled 30-millimeter chain gun and HJ-16 anti-tank missiles, enabling it to engage tanks, light armored vehicles and low-flying unmanned aerial vehicles, Wang Yunfei, a Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times on Sunday. The vehicle's protection has also been enhanced with a V-shaped mine-resistant hull, while modular composite armor can be fitted for additional protection. A ramp-style rear door allows infantry to get in and out of the vehicle more quickly, helping troops deploy more rapidly during combat operations, Wang said. The new vehicle's information systems can likely share battlefield information in real time with other platforms, including drones and artillery units, improving situational awareness and coordination among different elements of a combined-arms force. The vehicle is also adapted for operations in plateau environments, Wang said. The new vehicle retains the high mobility and amphibious capabilities of the 8x8 wheeled family, allowing it to move rapidly across different types of terrain and waterways. As a new-generation main combat vehicle for medium combined-arms brigades, it is designed to support rapid deployment and operations in plateau regions, border areas and areas with dense waterways, Wang noted. It also addresses some of the shortcomings of the Type 08 family, particularly in defensive and information systems. Its upgrades are expected to improve the sustained combat capabilities and survivability of the PLA's medium combined-arms brigades, according to Wang. Despite the introduction of the new vehicle, however, the Type 08 family is expected to remain an important part of the PLA's medium combined-arms brigades for years to come. Wang said the older vehicles would continue to undertake a substantial share of readiness and training tasks over roughly the next decade, while gradually handing over their leading role to the new-generation wheeled armored vehicle family over a longer period.

item.title: Chinese, Vietnamese navies complete 41st joint patrol in Beibu Gulf; move boosts maritime trust and risk control: expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-22 20:47:00
Photo: PLA Navy The Chinese and Vietnamese navies have successfully completed their 41st joint patrol in the Beibu Gulf over two days, covering 351 nautical miles in 32 hours and including a joint maritime search-and-rescue drill, the PLA Daily reported on Sunday. China and Vietnam's joint naval patrols as well as joint coast guard operations could help manage risks, foster mutual trust and resolve maritime differences. By boosting cooperation in the Beibu Gulf and upholding maritime security and order, the two sides are also consolidating cooperation in fisheries, shipping and maritime search and rescue, and contributing to peace, stability and development across the region, according to a Chinese military expert. During the joint patrol, China deployed the naval vessels Wuzhou and Enshi, while Vietnam sent two naval vessels to participate. The Chinese and Vietnamese vessels arrived in their designated patrol area in the Beibu Gulf on Friday. After establishing communications, the two sides patrolled in two parallel columns along the China-Vietnam demarcation line in the gulf, according to the PLA Daily. During the operation, the two sides transferred command authority in stages and exchanged data on courses, speeds and other operational details, maintaining real-time awareness of the maritime situation. On Saturday, the joint patrol fleet held a search-and-rescue drill simulating two fishing vessels in distress in the Beibu Gulf. After being informed that crew members had fallen overboard, the fleet adjusted its course and speed, drew up search-and-rescue plan and used multiple search methods to accurately locate and rescue the personnel in the water. After the exercise, the fleet practiced coordinated formation changes under agreed rules for alternating command, including single-column, single-line-abreast and double-column formations. Both sides maintained close communication and demonstrated smooth coordination throughout the drills. After completing all scheduled drills, the Chinese and Vietnamese vessels separated and departed in different directions. Personnel from both sides lined up in their respective areas and waved goodbye, marking the successful conclusion of the 41st China-Vietnam joint patrol. The choice of vessels on Chinese side underscores the non-confrontational nature of the joint patrols, which focus on maritime risk management, emergency response and confidence-building rather than military deterrence, Song Zhongping, a military affairs expert, told the Global Times on Sunday. The rotating command arrangement also reflects both sides' equal sovereign status while enhancing interoperability, mutual understanding and coordination, said Song. The PLA Daily cited a Chinese commander as saying that adding exercises to the joint patrol enhanced the two navies' ability to conduct coordinated operations and promoted professional exchanges and practical cooperation between the two sides. The China-Vietnam joint patrols in the Beibu Gulf are friendly exchanges conducted by the two militaries under relevant agreements and annual plans. The report said the patrols help strengthen friendship between the two countries, deepen mutual trust between the two militaries, and effectively enhancing both sides' ability to respond jointly to maritime emergencies and safeguard maritime security and stability. Song noted that China and Vietnam conduct joint naval patrols and coast guard law enforcement operations through separate, parallel mechanisms in the Beibu Gulf to manage maritime differences and prevent disputes from escalating. Regular communication channels, coordinated response protocols and frontline cooperation help reduce miscalculations, build military trust and strengthen crisis management. Since the signing of the Agreement on Joint Patrols by the Navies of China and Vietnam in the Beibu Gulf in 2005, these patrols have served as a stable platform for communication, helping both sides deepen cooperation and enhance strategic mutual trust, according to the Xinhua News Agency. The Chinese and Vietnamese coast guards conducted their first joint patrol in the Beibu Gulf for 2026 from April 22 to 24, marking the 30th joint patrol by the two countries' maritime law enforcement agencies since 2006. By strengthening cooperation in the Beibu Gulf, China and Vietnam are also upholding the spirit of the Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea (DOC), safeguarding maritime security and stability, and advancing cooperation in fisheries, shipping and search and rescue, said Song. Such coordination also supports broader economic and trade ties between the two countries, helping contain risks, build mutual trust and promote peace and development in the South China Sea and across Southeast Asia, the expert said.

item.title: China, US hold military maritime safety talks in Shanghai; dialogue helps reduce risks, promote stability: expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-20 23:42:00
China US Photo: VCG The Chinese and US militaries held the second working group meeting and annual meeting of the China-US Military Maritime Consultative Agreement (MMCA) mechanism for 2026 in Shanghai from Wednesday to Friday, according to a release by the Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) Navy on Friday. The two sides exchanged views on the current maritime and air security situation, reviewed the annual implementation of the Rules of Behavior for Safety of Air and Maritime Encounters, discussed measures to improve military maritime safety and security, and agreed on topics for the 2027 working group meeting. A Chinese military affairs expert said that regular maritime security dialogue between China and the US could help reduce miscalculations and friction, while effective communication and emergency response mechanisms could help the two sides address unexpected incidents and prevent tensions from escalating. The meeting was aimed at implementing the important consensus reached by the two countries' leaders and promoting the healthy, stable and sustainable development of military-to-military relations, the PLA Navy said. It followed a working group meeting under the same mechanism in Hawaii on May 28 and 29, when the two militaries reviewed the implementation of the air and maritime encounter rules since their 2025 meeting and discussed measures to improve military maritime safety. Observers noted that the Chinese and US militaries have kept communication channels open recently, as General Yang Zhibin, commander of the Chinese PLA Eastern Theater Command, had led a delegation to Victoria, Canada, to attend the 2026 Asia-Pacific Chiefs of Defense Conference jointly hosted by the Canadian Armed Forces and the US Pacific Command, according to Chinese defense ministry spokesperson Jiang Bin on September 4. The spokesperson said that the Chinese side delivered a keynote speech at the event, presenting China's stance and achievements in maintaining regional peace and stability, and proposing that regional countries enhance defense cooperation and jointly address common challenges. The Chinese delegation also held bilateral meetings with representatives, including those from the US. The two militaries also held their fourth Crisis Communication and Prevention Working Group meeting on November 2 and 3 in Washington DC. The two sides had an in-depth exchange of views on how to deliver on the consensus reached by the two presidents, strengthen communication, and avoid misunderstanding and miscalculation, Chinese Defense Ministry spokesperson Chen Xi said on November 13. He added that the two defense departments remained in communication and coordination over exchanges and dialogue at various levels. Song Zhongping, a military affairs expert, told the Global Times on Friday that the Chinese and US militaries could face complicated situations in maritime interactions, and any unintended incidents between the two militaries could have wider security implications, so there is a need to regularly refine rules and strengthen communication to prevent miscalculations from escalating tensions. The military exchanges come amid efforts to implement the consensus reached by the Chinese and US leaders. During a meeting with US President Donald Trump in Shenzhen on Thursday, Chinese President Xi Jinping said that the key to sustaining the current momentum of stable and positive growth in the relationship lies in taking actions to deliver on the consensus between the two presidents. The Chinese president said that communication between our teams should also keep pace. Differences that cannot be resolved for the time being should be managed in a constructive way, and escalation should be prevented. The two sides agreed to formulate an action plan on building a constructive relationship of strategic stability. At the trilateral summit with Russia and the US in Shenzhen on the same day, the Chinese leader called for regular high-level exchanges, keeping dialogue channels open at all levels, and establishing crisis communication and prevention mechanisms, to ensure that misjudgments occur less, differences can be managed, and frictions will not escalate. Following the summit, the leaders of China, Russia and the US issued the China-Russia-US Heads of State Declaration toward Peace, stating their commitment to maintaining strategic stability and international security. Song said that establishing and improving military risk-management, dialogue and hotline mechanisms between China and the US would help safeguard regional peace and stability. Song noted that the Asia-Pacific's role as a major engine of global economic growth and its overall peace and stability were closely linked to restraint and efforts by China and the US to avoid conflict and confrontation. Continued commitment to this approach is important for maintaining regional and global peace, he said.

item.title: Kazakhstan receives Y-9E transport aircraft from China, with expert seeing wider export potential
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-20 20:13:00
Y-9E transport aircraft Photo: Courtesy of AVIC SAIC Kazakhstan's Defense Ministry officially announced on Thursday that a Y-9E military transport aircraft has arrived in Almaty, joining the fleet of the military transport aviation of the Kazakhstan Armed Forces. A military affairs expert told the Global Times that the Chinese-made aircraft's mature technology, logistical advantages and competitive cost could give it promising prospects in the international market. The delivery was carried out as part of a planned renewal of the aircraft fleet. The new aircraft will expand capabilities for transporting personnel, military cargo, and materiel, according to a statement published on the ministry's website. In terms of its capabilities, the Y-9E occupies an intermediate position between the C-295, a European-made tactical transport aircraft, and the A400M, a European four-engine military transport aircraft, currently in service. Its arrival will allow more flexible planning of air transport operations based on route distance and cargo weight, according to the release. The Global Times learned that the Y-9E is an export-oriented transport aircraft developed from China's Y-9 platform to meet the requirements of overseas customers. It is designed to transport personnel, equipment and supplies, and features a long range, a spacious cargo compartment, substantial payload capacity and convenient loading and unloading. It can operate in challenging environments, including extreme heat, high altitudes and extreme cold. Publicly available information indicates that the Y-9E is approximately 36 meters long, with a wingspan of about 38 meters. It has a maximum payload of 20 metric tons and a maximum takeoff weight of approximately 65 tons. The aircraft has a maximum level-flight speed of around 660 kilometers per hour, a cruising altitude of 7,000 to 8,000 meters and a maximum range of 5,200 kilometers. The Y-9E is a further development of the Y-8 transport aircraft, with substantial improvements to its airframe structure, Wang Ya'nan, editor-in-chief of Beijing-based Aerospace Knowledge magazine, told the Global Times on Friday. The aircraft features a modern glass cockpit with upgraded avionics that meet mainstream international standards. The aircraft has also benefited from improvements in engine performance and aerodynamics, resulting in an increased payload capacity compared with the Y-8. The aircraft has been showcased at several international and domestic air shows and defense exhibitions, including the 2018 Singapore Airshow, the 15th China International Aviation and Aerospace Exhibition in Zhuhai, South China's Guangdong Province, in 2024, and the 2026 Africa Aerospace and Defence exhibition. Kazakhstan is the second known overseas customer for the Y-9E, following Namibia. In December 2024, the Namibian Air Force officially received two Y-9E medium military transport aircraft bought from China, according to the local media outlet The Namibian. One of the Y-9E's advantages in the export market is the fact that the Chinese People's Liberation Army itself operates the Y-9 in substantial numbers, with various special-mission aircraft also developed on the same platform, Wang said. This large domestic user base helps support higher production volumes, a mature technological foundation and a stable supply of spare parts and maintenance services, while also offering potential cost advantages to overseas customers. The expert added that the Y-9E could offer an alternative to countries seeking to replace aging medium-sized transport aircraft, such as the US-made C-130 Hercules. The C-130 has been in service for decades, but many countries seem to face the challenge of upgrading or replacing their aging fleets. Against this backdrop, the Y-9E offers another option for countries seeking a medium-sized military transport aircraft. Its performance may have won favor in many countries, potentially opening up broader opportunities for the Chinese aircraft in the international market, Wang said.

item.title: PLA Army develops artillery calibration robot to improve firing accuracy on plateaus
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-18 21:56:00
An artillery crew member assigned to an artillery unit of a brigade under the Chinese PLA Army uses a lanyard to fire the first round from a PLZ-89 self-propelled howitzer during a live-fire training exercise in early June, 2026. Photo: eng.chinamil.com.cn The PLA Daily on Wednesday reported on an intelligent artillery calibration robot developed by a regiment of the PLA Army. The innovation was driven by the urgent need at the grassroots level for faster and more accurate artillery calibration. After years of development and refinement, the system has significantly shortened firing preparation time while improving strike accuracy during plateau live-fire drills. According to the report, several years ago, after a new type of artillery piece was deployed to the regiment, a live-fire exercise on a plateau exposed problems with significant firing deviations and accuracy falling short of combat requirements. A comparative analysis found that the problems were caused by insufficient experience among some gunners and inadequate preparation for carrying out artillery calibration. To shorten calibration time and improve efficiency, Zhang Guozhu, a master sergeant second class of the regiment, proposed developing a rapid calibration system capable of operating in high-altitude environments. After more than 100 days of intensive work, the team developed an artillery sighting and calibration system for a specific type of self-propelled artillery, building on existing equipment already in service. The system received a national invention patent. The system effectively reduces firing deviations in high-altitude environments and improves artillery accuracy. It later became one of the core technologies underpinning the intelligent artillery calibration robot. While the first-generation calibration system addressed the key challenge of accuracy, its calculations still relied on multiple existing devices, making the process time-consuming. Further improvements involved a complex development process, including entering more than 3,000 sets of real-world data covering extreme cold, strong winds and high-altitude conditions into the system under harsh weather conditions. In July 2025, Zhang and researchers from the equipment manufacturer continued their efforts to upgrade and optimize the technology, further developing the intelligent artillery calibration robot. The system can automatically conduct technical inspections of artillery under different climatic and altitude conditions, build a basic database for each artillery piece, and generate comprehensive intelligent inspection reports. During repeated plateau live-fire exercises, the robot helped service members achieve new levels of speed and accuracy, earning the nickname "robot squad leader." Song Zhongping, a military affairs expert, told the Global Times that high-altitude environments pose considerable challenges to artillery operations, with multiple factors affecting firing accuracy. First, the sharp decline in air density at high altitudes can cause shells to drift and travel farther, making their dispersion less predictable. Second, significant vertical temperature gradients mean that shells pass through air layers at different altitudes and temperatures, which can also affect their trajectories. In addition, terrain that obstructs firing lines and changes in the performance of equipment and ammunition in a cold plateau environment can further contribute to firing deviations, Song said. The challenges are even more pronounced for personnel. Oxygen deprivation at high altitudes reduces physical endurance and slows down tasks such as observation and equipment setup, undermining overall operational capabilities. These factors compound one another, Song said. The expert explained that calibration has become a major weak link affecting artillery performance in high-altitude combat, primarily because establishing and calibrating fire-control reference points is particularly difficult in mountainous terrain. On plains, crews can find large, flat areas for calibration, whereas mountainous plateaus offer few suitable locations. Meteorological calibration is equally challenging. Conducting atmospheric soundings across vast plateau areas is complicated, while making localized weather corrections is also difficult. Song added that the lower air resistance at high altitudes allows artillery shells to travel farther, which is an advantage in itself. However, making full use of this advantage requires addressing a key challenge: While the firing range increases, changes in air density also alter the shells' trajectories. Proper calibration can help overcome this problem, significantly enhancing artillery's actual combat capabilities on the plateau. This is precisely the kind of challenge the intelligent calibration system is designed to address. A sergeant from a company said in the PLA Daily report that live-fire shooting in strong winds had previously been a major test of a gun commander's mental fortitude. With the new system, however, artillery can sustain stable firing even in extreme weather, enabling inexperienced personnel to achieve results comparable to those of seasoned crew members. A senior sergeant first class from a company said in the report that artillery crews previously devoted much of their time and energy to calibration and calculations. The robot has freed them to focus more on tactical assessments and fire coordination, significantly accelerating their response tempo. With the introduction of the robot, Song said, its accuracy, reliability and safety are expected to improve further as the system is refined and its database continues to expand. Explaining what prompted the development, Zhang said that new weapons such as drones had demonstrated their capabilities in several regional conflicts, profoundly reshaping perceptions of modern warfare. Continuing to approach things with traditional thinking will make it difficult to win during today's modern, smart warfare. As such, the army should step up research, he said.

item.title: PLA's drone family expands as state media details GJ-11's combat capability
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-16 22:28:00
The GJ-11 stealth drone Photo: Screenshot from CCTV News military channel After the Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) Air Force released more close-up footage of the GJ-11 stealth drone, Chinese state media CCTV recently offered further analysis of the aircraft. PLA drones have been frequently featured in media coverage recently, drawing growing attention. An expert said the PLA's formidable drone lineup appears to have a division of labor, but each type is actually moving toward multi-function roles, supporting the Air Force's strategic shift toward integrating air and space capabilities as well as coordinating offensive and defensive operations with new-quality combat forces. On Sunday, CCTV's military channel made note of the GJ-11's distinctive shape and large size. Military affairs commentator Zhang Xuefeng said in the report that preliminary estimates put its wingspan at or beyond that of some light fighters, with a takeoff weight over 10 tons. That size boosts range and combat radius, allows a larger weapons bay for more diverse munitions, and supports bigger payloads such as reconnaissance gear, improving overall capability and future upgrade potential. Zhang said that the GJ-11 has already scored a first-round hit in training, noting that the moment its munitions struck the target meant the drone had achieved combat capability. Zhang further explained that the GJ-11 can strike ground and sea targets and carry anti-ship munitions. It has an infrared electro-optical sensor window under its nose, with sensors typically including visible-light, infrared imaging and laser channels. Laser illumination means it can drop laser-guided bombs for greater accuracy. Its weapons bay can also carry loitering munitions to extend strike range, destroying enemy air defense systems beyond their effective detection range, therefore suppressing the enemy's air defense. The GJ-11 is just one of many new members of China's powerful domestic military drone family. CCTV said that in today's new era, as the PLA Air Force's combat system develops, new-quality combat forces such as drones keep advancing. Some models that have been frequently featured in media reports recently have shown advanced performance. Previously unseen footage of the WZ-7 high-altitude reconnaissance drone conducting a deterrence patrol over China's Huangyan Dao in the South China Sea was released by a CCTV program on Thursday. A WZ-7 high-altitude reconnaissance unmanned aerial vehicle Photo: Screenshot from the military channel of the CCTV News The WZ-7 is 14 meters long with a 22.8-meter wingspan and a distinctive aerodynamic diamond joined-wing layout. It can carry a synthetic aperture radar, high-resolution digital cameras, infrared thermal imaging equipment and electronic reconnaissance suites, giving it all-weather, round-the-clock reconnaissance capabilities. It can fly at altitudes up to 20,000 meters, which previously left Japanese military planes tracking it only able to shoot blurry photos from below, CCTV said. The WZ-8 is China's high-speed drone. Military affairs expert Du Wenlong said it uses a flying-wing layout and a rocket engine, enabling it to reach an altitude of 20,000 meters and a speed of Mach 2. To date, it is the only drone of its kind in the world. The WZ-10 is a domestically developed unmanned electronic reconnaissance aircraft. Mainly used for electronic reconnaissance missions, it is capable of intercepting and locating enemy radar signals, CCTV said. The shipborne variant of the GJ-11, the GJ-21, the PLA's first shipborne stealth reconnaissance-strike drone, uses a tailless flying-wing, blended wing-body layout with internal weapons bays and fuel space. It made its public debut at the September 3, 2025, V-Day parade. In late October, it successfully took off and landed on the Type 076 amphibious assault ship Sichuan , another breakthrough in China's amphibious assault ship development, marking the PLA Navy's capability to operate fixed-wing stealth drones from large maritime platforms. The previously mysterious GJ-3A armed reconnaissance drone only made its debut in an Army Day film in August. Along with the WZ-7 and WZ-10, it provides intelligence support to the PLA Army, Navy and Rocket Force. The GJ-3A armed reconnaissance drone, WZ-10 reconnaissance drone and WZ-7 reconnaissance drone together in a split-screen display Photo: Screenshot from CCTV News Wang Yanan, editor-in-chief of Beijing-based Aerospace Knowledge magazine, told the Global Times that the GJ-3A is a medium-altitude, long-endurance UAV. It can be seen as an enhanced and enlarged version of the Wing Loong, with a likely maximum takeoff weight exceeding 6 tons and a payload capacity of over 2 tons. It is not only capable of air-to-ground strikes but also possesses air-to-air combat capabilities. Song Zhongping, a Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times on Monday that while these models appear to have a division of labor, each is actually moving toward multi-function, multi-module and diversified roles. Reconnaissance-strike drones can also conduct effective detection missions, and stealth drones' penetration can be used for both attack and reconnaissance. Various drones can carry different modules for different functions, for example, adding a navigation module for real-time navigation of an area, or providing communications and relay guidance. In future air combat, manned-unmanned coordination may take two forms. One is crewed aircraft controlling drones to attack, detect and guide targets farther away. The other is true air-combat drones, which need highly advanced AI to effectively accompany crewed fighters as genuine unmanned wingmen. But such wingmen are still under development and not yet a reality, Song said. Beyond air combat, Wang added, the precision operational needs of each service are now closely tied to the massive intelligence data generated by drones. As drone applications in joint operations continue to expand, faster data processing and better intelligent algorithms will open unlimited possibilities for unmanned warfare. PLA drones are moving from single platforms toward a system-based operational architecture, showing a clear path for the Air Force's leap from competing in platforms to competing in systems, and for supporting its strategic transition toward integrated air and space, offense and defense, with new-quality combat forces, Song said.

item.title: Developer of China's J-35 series fighter jets uses 3D printing to advance warplane structural development, building lighter, stronger aircraft
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-14 15:00:00
A J-35 stealth fighter jet is ready to take off from China's first electromagnetic catapult-equipped aircraft carrier, the Fujian (Hull 18). Three types of aircraft recently completed their inaugural electromagnetic catapult-assisted takeoff and arrested landing trainings on the aircraft carrier.(eng.chinamil.com.cn/Photo by Ju Zhenhua) As aviation equipment advances toward lighter, higher-performance and multifunctional designs, 3D printing is emerging as a key technology for overcoming traditional manufacturing constraints. A key laboratory at AVIC Shenyang Aircraft Design and Research Institute, the developer of China's J-35 series fighter jets, has made breakthroughs in the practical application of 3D printing in aircraft development, according to a WeChat post by the Aviation Industry Corporation of China (AVIC) on Saturday. In traditional aircraft structural development, design and manufacturing are often disconnected. This approach can lead to development delays, excessive weight and cost overruns, making it difficult to meet the growing demand for lightweight, high-efficiency, long-lasting, multifunctional and cost-effective aircraft structures that can be developed rapidly. The advances in 3D printing technology at the Key Laboratory of Aviation Science and Technology for Novel Aircraft Structures under AVIC's Shenyang Aircraft Design and Research Institute are helping overcome the constraints of conventional manufacturing, enabling greater design flexibility and more efficient aircraft structural development, according to the release. AVIC's Shenyang Aircraft Design and Research Institute, China's first aircraft design and research institute, has undertaken the development of more than 40 major aviation equipment models across five series, including the J-8, J-11, J-15, J-35 and unmanned aircraft, according to people.com.cn. "With no need for molds, rapid production capabilities and the ability to fabricate complex structures, 3D printing plays an important role in aircraft development. It enables the integration of design and manufacturing, as well as structure and function, giving designers greater freedom," Cui Can, deputy director of the laboratory, was quoted by the AVIC release as saying. Cui added that 3D printing serves as a key accelerator, particularly during the prototyping of new aircraft, allowing a wide range of innovative structural designs to be rapidly turned into physical components for testing and evaluation. 3D printing technology is driving the manufacturing of large aircraft structures toward greater integration. In recent years, the laboratory has achieved breakthroughs in developing primary load-bearing aircraft structures, successfully producing an integrated structural component measuring more than five meters in length using 3D printing technology. Located in the aircraft's central fuselage, the component primarily serves to bear and transfer structural loads, according to AVIC. Installed inside an aircraft's air intake, the 3D-printed multifunctional annular heat exchanger integrates heat transfer, air extraction, load-bearing and maintenance functions. With the help of 3D printing technology, the research team also incorporated manufacturing requirements into the design process from the outset, developing complex internal flow channels that increase the heat transfer surface area while reducing the component's weight. Turning a successfully printed laboratory prototype into a component suitable for actual aircraft applications required overcoming major challenges in manufacturing and engineering validation. To address thermal stress, deformation and cracking during the printing of large components, the team developed an innovative process combining segmented component printing and additive fusion joining. To overcome difficulties in finishing the intricate internal channels of the annular heat exchanger, the researchers independently developed a specialized magnetic grinding device. By placing fine steel needles inside the flow channels and controlling their movement with an external magnetic field, the device enables the needles to slide, tumble and polish the internal surfaces without damaging the structure. Over more than two decades, the laboratory has pursued a path of innovation, progressing from technological exploration to engineering applications and from individual breakthroughs to the development of comprehensive technological capabilities. To date, it has successfully applied six additive manufacturing processes, 13 types of metal materials and 19 categories of 3D-printed structural components in aircraft development programs, said the release. The team has established a comprehensive technological development framework encompassing the incubation of novel structural concepts, breakthroughs in key technologies and engineering development. These efforts have helped overcome technical bottlenecks in aircraft development and advance innovation in aircraft structural technologies. The continued advancement and wider application of 3D printing technology have made innovative structural concepts a reality, including large-scale integrated structures, topology-optimized configurations, functionally graded composite structures and the integration of structural and functional capabilities. These advances are expected to enhance the overall performance and quality of airframe structures while supporting China's pursuit of self-reliance and strength in aviation science and technology. Global Times

item.title: Chinese and US defense establishments maintain coordination on dialogues at different levels: Chinese defense ministry
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-13 15:11:00
Chen Xi, spokesperson of China's Ministry of National Defense The Chinese and US militaries held the 4th Crisis Communication and Prevention Working Group meeting on November 2-3 in Washington, D.C.. The two sides had an in-depth exchange of views on how to deliver on the consensus reached by the two presidents, strengthen communication, and avoid misunderstanding and miscalculation, Chen Xi, a spokesperson of the Ministry of National Defense said on Friday. Chen made the remarks when asked to provide further updates on China-US military-to-military engagement. According to a readout from the US Department of Defense, the US and Chinese militaries held a Crisis Communication and Prevention Working Group meeting in Washington, D.C.. Sources also indicate that the US Secretary of Defense and the Commander of the US Pacific Command might soon visit China. Chen said that building a stable, healthy and sustainable relationship between the Chinese and US militaries serves the shared interests of both sides and is a common expectation of the international community. The Chinese side values strategic communication with the US military, and the two defense establishments have maintained coordination on dialogues at different levels. We hope the US side will work with us to follow through on the important consensus reached by the two presidents, enhance communication, and properly manage differences, so as to add positive factors to building a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability, said Chen. item.title: J-35A marks 2nd anniversary of its debut; state media analyzes upgrade prospects, including full version of WS-19 engine
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-12 22:15:00
A full-scale model of the J-35A stealth fighter sits on display at the Dajiaochang Airport Runway Park in Nanjing, East China's Jiangsu Province, on November 10, 2026. Photo: VCG Thursday marked two years since the J-35A, China's domestically developed medium stealth multi-role fighter, made its public debut. As a new-generation stealth fighter, the J-35A has achieved key upgrades in avionics, situational awareness and weapons integration. State media CCTV News analyzed its upgrade prospects, mentioning an expected switch to using the full version of the domestically developed WS-19 turbofan engine. The J-35A, officially codenamed Yunlong (Cloud Dragon/Loong), is a single-seat, twin-engine fighter and the second type of fifth-generation stealth fighter jet independently developed by China, featuring the PLA Air Force's experience with and feedback on the J-20, China's first type of stealth fighter jet. The J-35A was designed with a balanced consideration of performance, reliability, maintainability and cost in mind, Wang Ya'nan, editor-in-chief of Beijing-based Aerospace Knowledge magazine, told the Global Times. For stealth, the J-35A uses an integrated low-observable design rather than relying on coatings alone. Its configuration features a blended wing body, twin canted vertical tails, all-moving horizontal tails and a diverterless supersonic inlet (DSI) to reduce radar reflections. Bay door seams follow edge-alignment principles, and integrated precision manufacturing reduces gap scattering. The cockpit canopy is coated with a conductive stealth film to compress radar returns, achieving multi-directional stealth, introduced CCTV. The radar cross section (RCS) of China's J-35 series is extremely small, thanks to its special fuselage design and China-exclusive metamaterial technologies, Wang noted. Such a small RCS allows the J-35 to remain undetected until it is very close to its target, giving it more advantages and opportunities in combat. This also means the J-35's stealth capability is at a world-class level. When it comes to avionics and situational awareness, the J-35A carries a new-generation active electronically scanned array radar, offering longer detection range and some capability against stealth targets. An electro-optical window under the nose provides electro-optical detection. The system supports sensor fusion and links with the pilot's helmet-mounted display, and can network with the J-20 and drones via high-speed data links, said CCTV. Military commentator Shao Yongling said in the CCTV News report that concerning weapons integration, the J-35A has an internal weapons bay for medium-range and short-range air-to-air missiles in stealth mode. The wings also have external hardpoints for air-to-ground and anti-ship munitions in non-stealth mode. With the public debut of the J-35A in November 2024, the Air Force's traditional "three swordsmen," the J-20 stealth fighter, J-16 fighter and J-10C fighter, have expanded and upgraded into a new "four swordsmen" lineup that includes two types of stealth fighters. The four "swordsmen" form a new combination in the Air Force's new-quality aviation combat power, CCTV reported. Shao noted that the J-20 is a high-end heavy fighter for high-value targets, while the J-35A is a medium fighter. They complement each other with clear differences in design and mission. The J-35A is smaller, cheaper and easier to maintain, making it better suited for large-scale fielding as a scalable, general-purpose stealth fighter. Its first core mission is routine air patrol and regional air defense. The second is multi-mission strikes: In stealth mode it can penetrate defenses and hit air defense sites, radars and ships; when needed, it switches to non-stealth mode with more munitions for air-to-ground and anti-ship support. It also supports system-based distributed operations, Shao said. China's J-35A fighter jet carries out its first adaptive training session at Zhuhai Jinwan Airport on November 8, 2024, ahead of the 15th China International Aviation and Aerospace Exhibition, also known as Airshow China, to be held in Zhuhai, South China's Guangdong Province. Photo: VCG In system confrontations, Shao said, once the J-20 opens a gap, large numbers of J-35As network with early warning aircraft and unmanned wingmen for wide-area surveillance and forward reconnaissance. Operating with fourth-generation fighters such as the J-16 and J-10C, the J-35A can slip in first to locate enemy radar and air defense sites and share coordinates with the rest of the formation, bringing stealth reconnaissance plus target guidance, the expert added. Despite these strengths, the CCTV report said the J-35A is far from the end point. From the start, it was designed with ample room for expansion of its capabilities. "A two-seat variant is technically feasible, and its core value would be as a command platform for unmanned wingmen. However, no official project has been announced. Besides a two-seat version, I think an electronic warfare variant is also an option," Shao was quoted by CCTV as saying. As for foreseeable upgrades to the J-35A, Shao sees four areas. First, the engine switching to the full version of the WS-19 turbofan engine. Second, Shao noted avionics and intelligence, which involves strengthening detection of stealth targets and reducing pilot workload through smarter systems. Third comes weapons and a bay expansion, which means optimizing the internal bay for more new munitions and a richer stealth-mode strike list. Finally, iterative stealth refinements will see improving stealth stability in complex environments. Overall, the J-35A is unlikely to pursue all-round upgrades at once, and will probably follow a "small-step, fast-iteration" path in batches, Shao said. Wang Yongqing, the chief designer of multiple types of aircraft as well as the chief expert of the Shenyang Aircraft Design and Research Institute under AVIC, previously described the J-35 series' development approach in an interview with Global Times. He said the J-35 series, developed with an "air-sea twin configuration" approach and a "one aircraft, multiple variants" concept, is expected to enter large-scale production in the future, with the aircraft acting as a "point guard" in systematic combat operations and delivering outstanding performance.
